summary: The Priest-Elders: the most peopled of the four southern isles, with a ruined shrine beneath the tide and a name carved over its door.

old_rite.name: The Old Rite
old_rite.desc: The priests chant at dawn and dusk in a tongue nobody speaks, and the chant is taught to every child. Nobody knows what the words mean, and nobody has ever asked to stop.

eldest_priest.name: The Eldest Priest
eldest_priest.desc: The eldest of the priest-elders leads the rite and rules the island, and his staff is carved with every name the rite has kept. His word is law because it is also prayer.

low_tide_rite.name: The Low-Tide Rite
low_tide_rite.desc: At the lowest tides the priests walk down the causeway to the drowned shrine and chant the name carved above its door. The island gathers on the shore to listen.

shrine_wardens.name: The Shrine Wardens
shrine_wardens.desc: Wardens keep watch over the drowned shrine from boats and rocks, in turns, from tide to tide. Nobody touches the stones, and nobody sleeps near them.

island_levy.name: The Island Levy
island_levy.desc: Every terrace village keeps a muster-roll and a stack of spears, and the priests bless both at the rite. The island is crowded, and its sons are many.

the_low_tide_rite.title: The Low-Tide Rite
the_low_tide_rite.desc: At the lowest tide of the year the priests walk down to the drowned shrine and chant the old name. The island watches from the shore, as it has always done, and the children are told to be quiet.

options.name: Keep the rite as our fathers did
Ask the old ones what the name means

scholars_at_the_shrine.title: Scholars at the Shrine
scholars_at_the_shrine.desc: Scholars from the Deliverer's temples ask leave to copy the old inscription for their libraries. They are courteous, well supplied and very patient, and they do not say why they want it.

the_name_is_answered.title: The Name Is Answered
the_name_is_answered.desc: Word comes that the stranger has named himself in the courts of the north: Eindil, son of Ein, grandson of Aen. The priests of the drowned shrine now know whose name they have been chanting.

options.name: Send our priests to tell the world

focuses.name: The Priest-Elders
focuses.desc: Enhis Is Rond is the most peopled of the southern isles, a round terraced island ruled by priest-elders. Priest-Elder Enhis keeps the rite and the law, and finds little difference between them.

focuses.name: The Old Rite
focuses.desc: The rite is sung at dawn and dusk on every terrace, and the chant is older than any priest-elder's memory. It binds the island together as a rope binds a boat.

focuses.name: The Council of Priests
focuses.desc: The priests sit in a ring in the temple court, each with a staff, and speak in order of age. The youngest speak last and are heard most closely.

focuses.name: The Island Law
focuses.desc: The island's law is taught to children as a chant, so that no one can claim not to know it. A dispute is settled when both sides can recite the same verse.

focuses.name: The Eldest Priest
focuses.desc: The oldest of the priests takes the staff and the title, and rules the island from the temple court. He is never alone, for the rite is always with him.

focuses.name: The Shrine Beneath the Tide
focuses.desc: Off the southern shore a ruined shrine stands beneath the tide, its door carved with a name. At the lowest tides the priests walk down to it and chant the name, as their fathers did.

focuses.name: The Low-Tide Rite
focuses.desc: A causeway of laid stones is built to the shrine, passable only at the lowest tide. The rite is held there each year, and the island gathers on the shore to hear it.

focuses.name: Divers of the Shrine
focuses.desc: Pearl-divers are trained to work the waters round the shrine, and told never to touch the stones. They bring up shells, sand and sometimes a worked bead.

focuses.name: Copy the Inscription
focuses.desc: The priests copy the name over the door onto sheets of bark and clay, and send the copies to the temple library. They repeat it with care and cannot explain it.

effects.tooltip: The priests copy a name they repeat but do not understand.

focuses.name: Scholars at the Shrine
focuses.desc: Visiting scholars ask leave to study the shrine, bringing paper, ink and a generous letter. The priest-elders admit them to the causeway and keep one eye on their notes.

focuses.name: The Shrine Wardens
focuses.desc: Wardens are appointed from the oldest families to guard the drowned shrine. They serve for life and are buried in sight of it.

focuses.name: The Stranger Reads the Stones
focuses.desc: A stranger from the sea read the old stones with our priests and went away quiet. He asked only how the name was sung, and he sang it back to them correctly.

effects.tooltip: A stranger from the sea read the old stones with our priests and went away quiet.

focuses.name: Carry the Name to Gala
focuses.desc: The priests copy the name and its story onto cedar slats, and send them south to Gala in a sealed chest. A tale too old for any man to explain may be understood by those who live long.

effects.tooltip: A tale too old for any man to explain goes south to Gala.

focuses.name: The Name Is Answered
focuses.desc: The name over the shrine door has an answer, and the priests have heard it. They sing the rite again that night, and the words mean something at last.

focuses.name: The Crowded Isle
focuses.desc: More people live on this round island than on any of its neighbours, and every hillside is terraced to the top. The priests count them at the rite and write the number in the temple book.

focuses.name: Terraced Villages
focuses.desc: Villages climb the terraces in steps, each with its own well and shrine. Craftsmen set up their workshops along the lowest terrace, where the roads are widest.

focuses.name: The Island Levy
focuses.desc: Every village keeps a muster-roll and a stack of spears, and the priests bless both at the rite. The levy is large, quiet and very rarely called.

focuses.name: Many Hands
focuses.desc: A crowded island has many hands, and the priests find work for them all: weavers, potters, rope-makers and masons. No one is idle for long.
